title: Expanding the Bandwidth of Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles the deceptively hard problem of gauging who on a team actually has capacity to take on more work. The author explains why simply asking team members is unreliable, since some always say yes regardless of true capacity while others always say no, and why relying purely on past performance metrics falls short as well. The article's key contribution is a shift in framing: rather than treating bandwidth as fixed and searching for who happens to have spare capacity, the best leaders actively create bandwidth by reassigning, postponing, or reprioritizing existing tasks for the person best suited to new work. Bandwidth is presented as something leaders can grow through deliberate choices, not just discover through assessment.
points: The essay identifies a measurement problem most leaders underestimate: self-reported capacity is unreliable because some team members always say yes and others always say no.
It distinguishes assessing bandwidth (a diagnostic step) from creating bandwidth (an active leadership intervention), treating the latter as the more important skill.
Specific mechanisms for creating bandwidth — removing a task, delaying it, or reassigning it — give the concept an operational, not just conceptual, edge.
The closing framing, that bandwidth is 'an intellectual asset... one that leaders are capable of growing,' reframes capacity as a leadership output rather than a fixed team trait.
quotes: Determining who has the bandwidth to take on more right now and who doesn’t is one of the most critical assessments leaders make.

Ask some team members if they can take on more, and they will always say Yes. They will do whatever it takes to perform for the team and leader and agree to more, even when this is a disservice to their well-being.
So, relying solely on what team members say they can do often creates task inequity on the team.

They do this by taking a current assignment off their plate, temporarily postponing or delaying a task, lowering or rearranging existing priorities, or assigning one of their tasks to someone else on the team.
Bandwidth is an intellectual asset, one that leaders are capable of growing.
